My official engagement started in 1991 when I was invited to attend a drill and when I was issued with a uniform of the MUP of the Republic of Serbia. I was also issued with personal weapons, a pistol, M53, and a rifle, Zastava 72.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now you seem to be, in answering this question, offering to provide your military booklet. Is that correct, that you were offering to provide your military booklet to substantiate what you were saying back in the Stanisic case?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: My military booklet is still with the Ministry of Interior of the Republic of Serbia with the police brigade there. And there's also my personnel file with Mr. Zivorad Jovanovic. Both the Trial Chamber and the Defence can request for these two to be delivered to them, as well as my file where you can see where I was issued with the uniform, when I was issued with my personal weapons and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, that's a little bit different from what you said in the Stanisic case, isn't it? Because there, you seem to be offering to provide the booklet. Doesn't that imply that you've got the booklet at that time? It's under your control?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I did not have my military booklet. It is in the MUP of Serbia. I said then that I could provide it to the Trial Chamber. I can obtain the military booklet. I cannot obtain my file or the file for the weapons that I had been issued with. However, anybody, including myself, can get hold of my personal booklet.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And in early 19 -- in early July 1991, you were told that you would be going to train in Bubanj Potok; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Was Bubanj Potok a JNA camp?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Bubanj Potok was a JNA military post and barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And when you arrived there, you were told that you would be assigned to a unit called the police brigade; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. A small correction: I was not told I would be assigned. I was already a member of the police brigade. I had already been issued with a uniform and personal weapons; a pistol to be more precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And in addition to your unit, there were also JNA conscripts, JNA volunteers training at Bubanj Potok; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And there were members of the SRS, the Serbian National Renewal, and the White Eagles. They were also all training at Bubanj Potok. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: As I've already told you, in 1991, when people got call-up papers for the JNA, only very few people responded and those were the people who were on the records of the Secretariat of Defence. So some parties, including the Serbian Radical Party and the Serbian National Renewal, and the Mirko Jovic's party, organised their own members who then volunteered as members of the reserve force of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And that training continued, as you testified earlier today at page 21, in 1992 and 1993; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That training continued in 1992 and in 1993. As I already stated in my statement, the government of the Republic of Serbia had issued a decree which was applied at check-points around the city of Belgrade and in the city itself. Persons who were of military age and who were capable of serving in the Army of the Serbian Krajina and the Army of Republika Srpska were brought to police stations and from there, they would be taken to the Bubanj Potok barracks where they were trained, equipped, and deployed in various areas or, rather, in the areas from which they hailed respectively.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And aside from volunteers who had been brought by the SRS, the SNO, or the White Eagles, did you hear about any other groups of volunteers who were trained at Bubanj Potok?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: The Serbian Radical Party and the Serbian Renewal Movement and the Matica of the Serbian emigrants did not bring people to the Bubanj Potok barracks directly. They suggested that people went to the Secretariat of National Defence in their municipalities and then they, in turn, assigned them either to the Bubanj Potok barracks or some other barracks for training. Around Belgrade, those were in Stara Pazova, in Zemun and Belgrade municipalities. Those who hailed from those municipalities were usually assigned and sent to the Bubanj Potok barracks, so one cannot say that the Serbian Radical Party or the Serbian Renewal Movement brought them directly to the Bubanj Potok barracks. Rather, they suggested that if their men were to volunteer, that they should report to their own Secretariat of Defence in their municipalities and then the secretariats would send them to undergo training either in the Bubanj Potok barracks or some other barracks. It all depended on what municipalities they came from, or rather, where they resided at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And did they train separately along -- in accord with their -- with the affiliation that you've mentioned, namely, SRS, SNO and White Eagles, or did they train together with everyone else, like any other JNA volunteer?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: They didn't have any separate training as members of the parties. It didn't depend on their affiliation with the -- either SRS or the SN -- they trained together with the regular JNA forces, whereas us, MUP members of the Republic of Serbia, had our own separate training. We did not train together with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And those various volunteers, were they attired in JNA reserve uniforms, regardless of their affiliation, party affiliation?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: In the Bubanj Potok barracks, they were all attired in JNA uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now I go back to a question I asked a little bit earlier. Aside from the three groups that you've mentioned of party-affiliated volunteers, did you hear about any other group of volunteers who trained at Bubanj Potok? And let me put it to you precisely. Did you ever hear about Arkan's men, the Serbian Volunteer Guard, training at Bubanj Potok?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: The Serbian Volunteer Guard, as far as I knew, were not in training in Bubanj Potok. They were recruited from other sources. I don't know how and where from. There was another unit under the command of the late Giska Bozovic. It had been set up by the Serbian Renewal Movement. They were independent from both the Serbian Volunteer Guard and the JNA. They set up their own unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, in your statement - and, if necessary, we can call it up - at paragraph 27, you refer to Zarko Sljukic as lieutenant-colonel. Did he have the rank of lieutenant-colonel at that point in time, in July 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, why did you put down that designation, lieutenant-colonel?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zarko Sljukic, in either 1993 or 1994, I can't remember the exact year, became lieutenant-colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now you say in your statement at paragraph 36, and we can turn to this, that the unit was transferred to Croatian territory across the --

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt. But, yeah, if we are going to keep referring to paragraphs of the statement, then in line what Your Honour said earlier, I think it would be fair to put it in front of the witness so he can read for himself, and that will facilitate proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, that's why I said we can turn to this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Does the witness have the statement in front of him?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, could I ask that we display it on the screen?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: We can.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So at paragraph 36, it says: "The unit was transferred to Croatian territory across the Danube by ferries at night. This all happened at the end of July and in early August 1991. We crossed into Croatian territory near Erdut in the morning and went to the Croatian SUP training centre, which had already been taken by Serbian forces." Now that Croatian SUP training centre that you refer to, is that the training centre that later came to be occupied by Arkan, amongst others?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And am I right in understanding this paragraph that you're saying that you went to the training centre on the same day that you arrived in Croatia, on the ferry?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We arrived in the course of the night.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And then that same morning, or the following morning, that's when you went to the training centre; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And how big was your unit at this time? Did it have a large convoy of vehicles? What -- what are you referring to when you say "your unit"?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: In terms of numbers, that unit had some 50 to 60 men. That was its composition.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So do I understand that it was only the men who crossed in ferries? No vehicles came with you.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Three vehicles crossed, a Lada Niva, and two Puch vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we call up 1D446, please, which is Defence tab 34. And if we could zoom in, please, a little bit tighter on the location where we see the bridge crossing the river. I think there's only one bridge that crosses the river. There we go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This is the Bogojevo bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Can you indicate on this photograph -- and perhaps he can do so the pointer and make a mark. Can you indicate on this photograph where it was that you left Serbia from and where it was that you arrived on the Croatian side?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: We were on the left bank of the Danube. I can't remember where exactly. But I know that it -- where we crossed the Danube river was about 1 to 2 kilometres from the bridge itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Did you engage in any fighting on the morning of your arrival, or that night?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: What did you do during the time between your arrival and the time that you go to the training centre?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, it was a long time ago, almost 20 years ago, we crossed from one bank to the other. We spent about two or three hours there, waiting for everybody to gather, and that's when we headed for the training centre in Erdut.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And that was the very day, wasn't it, that the JNA rolled across the bridge that we see on the photograph in front of us and took control of most of the area that we can now see in this photo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: When the JNA crossed the bridge, that territory had already been liberated. I can't remember when that was. I don't know when the JNA liberated the bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Are you saying the bridge wasn't in the control of JNA forces on the day that you arrived in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't say that the bridge was not in JNA control when we arrived in Croatia. I said that I didn't know who was in control of the bridge when we arrived in Croatia. Later on, as I was deployed in the area, it was the military police and the Serbian Volunteer Guard that controlled the bridge on the Croatian side.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: We'll come to that claim. But we have information, Mr. Kovacevic, that the JNA rolled across that bridge on the very same day that it took control of this territory, including the training centre. So what I'm asking you is: If the JNA controls this bridge on the same day that it controls the training centre and you go to the training centre on that day, why didn't your unit just drive across the bridge?

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Well, just to interject. I didn't recall the witness confirming that he could say it was the same day that the JNA controls the bridge that they went to the training centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, is the Prosecution contesting that the training centre was taken control of on the same day that the bridge was taken control of?

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Well, the question presupposes that the witness has confirmed that he goes to the training centre on the same day that the JNA controls the bridge which the witness, I believe, said he could not specifically recall. So there is an implicit assumption in the question which the witness hasn't confirmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: That's true, Mr. President. The witness hasn't confirmed it, but I indicated to the witness that we heard evidence to that effect and that was the basis for the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: You're right, Mr. Gosnell. That's, indeed, what you asked the witness. So please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, do you -- Mr. Kovacevic, do you have an answer? Why didn't you just cross the bridge along with JNA forces?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I can't answer your question, unfortunately. My unit that crossed the river consisted of us reservists and active policemen who were on temporary contracts in the MUP of the Republic of Serbia. They had joined from the MUP of the Republic of Croatia, because they were of Serb ethnicity. Now, as to why we didn't use the bridge, I didn't know then, I don't know now. My officers who were there just carried out orders that they had received. Why we didn't use the bridge, for what reason, I did not have any specific knowledge about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Was there a landing area where you were able to disembark your vehicles?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Those were three all-terrain vehicles, one Puch and Lada Nivas. And as we stopped at the bank of the Danube, we unrolled them. Those are vehicles that can drive on all terrains except water.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now at paragraph 36 you say that the training centre had already been taken by Serbian forces. Which Serbian forces specifically had taken the training centre, as far as you were able to learn or observe?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I was able to see at that moment, we were there, there were the Serbian Volunteer Guards and some other men. Maybe they were members of the Territorial Defence of Western Srem and Baranja; I couldn't know. We stayed there for just two or three days before we were transferred to Vera village.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Were JNA personnel present there too?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were some.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Who and how many?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I cannot tell you exactly who they were and how many because personnel came and went every day. So I can't know how many of them there were. I can't even tell you how many members of the Serbian Volunteer Guards and others were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: You say that you spent two to three days there. That's some period of time. Did you remain there continuously for those two to three days, or what were your activities?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: We prepared for transfer. We were packing our equipment, our gear. We were expecting some more gear that we needed to move to the village. Commanding officers had their own preparations, meetings, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Was your commander Sljukic there?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: No. Commander Sljukic was assigned to me at Vera village, when we arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Who was your commander at the time that you arrived at the training centre?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: The commander of that unit was Stevo Pavkovic, who had joined the MUP of Serbia coming from Zagreb, from the MUP of Croatia. And he was a native of a place called Srb in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Did you see Badza at the training centre for those two to three days that you were there?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't see him. However, my commanding officer went to meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, I'm now confining my question to those two to three days that you were there. Did anyone appear to be in charge at the training centre when you were there?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: It seemed to me that somebody was running the centre, because there was organisation. There was a schedule for breakfast, lunch, dinner, and activities were organised according to a roster.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, I'll come back to this question a little bit later. But after the two to three days that you spend at the training centre, as I understand it, you go to Vera and you're based in Vera for 45 days approximately; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's where I was billeted in a house at the very entrance to the village. In the centre of the village, you take a right turn to get to that house, and that was the third or the fourth house from the end of the village on the right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Did you ever hear that that was, in fact, the house of a Serb who had left Vera, was away, and gave permission for the house to be used?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I was not billeted in a house belonging to a Serb who had left Vera. I was billeted there together with another three or four men, and there was a 65-year-old lady in that house too.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, 45 days, as I understand it, you arrived in Croatia around the beginning of August. Forty-five days would take us up to the middle of September; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: My stint lasted until the fall of Vukovar. That means up to the 20th or the 21st. Perhaps three or four days after the fall of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, that wasn't my question. My question was: If you stayed in Vera for 45 days and you arrived in Croatia at the beginning of August, that means that the end of the 45 days occurs around the middle of September; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I spent 45 days in the village of Vera. Officially, it was entered in my military booklet that I arrived in that area sometime early in September or October, whereas the period when we actually arrived beginning with the -- early August was not written into the military booklet. I spent 45 days there, and after those 45 days, I was transferred to Brsadin.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Yeah, that was my -- that was going to be my next question. Did you spend the remainder of your time before you left Croatia based in Brsadin, after Vera?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: It's not exactly until the end. When the final operations to liberate Vukovar started, I joined the units that started from Brsadin via the woods in Luzac towards Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, when did you leave Brsadin?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I cannot remember exactly, but I think it was sometime after the 9th of November. Because I remember the 9th of November was some saint's day, Saint Mitar's Day, so it was around 9 or 10 November.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we have the witness's statement back on the screen, please. And if we could go, please, to paragraph 38.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kovacevic, you say that -- here that from Vera, your unit was sent towards Pacetin, Bobota, Brsadin, Marinci, and Bogdanovci. "When Brsadin and Brsadin silo were liberated, they became a base for the JNA and all the units located in that area, the JNA, police, and volunteers." Now when do you say that Brsadin village was liberated?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I cannot recall exactly when it was liberated. Brsadin village, I mean. Because I was not involved in the operations to liberate Brsadin or the Brsadin silo. So I could not pin-point it in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: How many kilometres is Brsadin from Vera, where you were based?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I cannot tell exactly because we came from Vera village to the observation post at Brsadin silo by dirt tracks, not the regular road.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Isn't it true that Brsadin was never in Croatian hands?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Whether it was in Croatian hands or not, I don't know. All I know is that the Brsadin silo was occupied by Croatian forces, whether the Home Guards Corps or the Croatian MUP, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, you say you don't know, and yet here in your statement at paragraph 38 in black and white, you say: "When Brsadin and the Brsadin silo were liberated ..." Now this is a statement that you not only signed but now three times you've come before Trial Chambers and said that, under oath, this is correct and accurate information. Is it correct and accurate information?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I said I did not participate in the liberation of Brsadin or the Brsadin silo, but I told you exactly that when the Brsadin silo was liberated, my unit and other units came there, and a centre for observation was formed there towards Vukovar, Luzac, and the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Why did you say something in your statement that you don't know whether is true or untrue? In fact, you don't seem to know anything about it at all and yet there it is in your statement. How can that happen?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I said I was not directly involved in the fighting to liberate Brsadin and the Brsadin silo. I know preparations and agreements were made with units of the Novi Sad Corps and the Territorial Staff of Slavonia, Western Srem, and Baranja. I don't know about the course of that operation. I was not involved. I don't know how it was carried out. All I know is that later when the Brsadin silo was liberated, several days later we moved and installed equipment at the Brsadin silo, equipment for observation and communication with all of the units deployed in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I think our time is up for this session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, Mr. Gosnell. Mr. Witness, we take our second break. We'll come back at 12.45. The court usher will escort you out of the courtroom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If we could turn to paragraph 16 of the witness's statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, in your statement at paragraph 16, you say that people in Croatia started arming themselves, which under the constitution they had a right to do. Now I have a few questions for you, and I think these can be answered yes or no. When you say that they had had a right to do this under the constitution, does that mean that you understood the constitution to confer a right on all citizens to take up arms to defend the territorial integrity of the country?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Under the constitution, every citizen of the then-Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was required to defend the territorial integrity of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And an attempted cessation by a republic was a threat to that territorial integrity; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And when a citizen takes up arms in defence of the country, they're considered a part of the TO, correct, unless they managed to join the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Well, before the war in the Socialist Federal Republic, in addition to the National Defence, we had civilian protection, and the Territorial Defence of the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now my point is, if you take up arms in defence of the country in a time of crisis, including an attempt by a republic to secede, if you don't manage to join the JNA as a volunteer, you're part of the TO. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And the TO was considered part of the armed forces of the SFRY; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And TOs, regardless of their exact regional base or description, were understood to be subordinate to the JNA units in whose zone of responsibility that TO unit is operating. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: This is something that anyone who does their compulsory JNA service, as you did, would know. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, if we could go to paragraph 41, please, of the statement, I want to ask you a few questions about the chain of command in relation to your unit, as you were able to observe it. And at paragraph 41, you say: "Some of our orders concerned police work, such as bringing in looters, while other orders had to do with combat action. Radovan Stojicic, Badza, commanded our units. We received orders for combat action from the JNA but Radovan Stojicic, Badza, had to be informed of these orders and approve them before we were allowed to act upon them. Our commander, Zarko Sljukic, received his orders from Lieutenant-Colonel Vaskovic, from the Ruma division and from his deputy Mrdja, also a lieutenant-colonel, when we were active in their zone of responsibility. He received some of the orders from Major-General Bratic, commander of the Novi Sad Corps. The late General Bratic and his deputy maintained contact with us. As far as we were concerned, Radovan Stojicic, Badza, was above Bratic because he could decide not to carry out an order from the JNA and because we submitted daily reports directly to Radovan Stojicic ..." I just want to clarify one or two points that arise from that statement. Now, first of all, we can agree, I think, that Badza has no authority, command authority over anyone in the JNA; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And did you ever hear of any occasion when Radovan Stojicic, Badza, refused to carry out an order that he had received from Bratic or Biorcevic?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I never heard directly that the late General Radovan Stojicic, Badza, refused an order from the late General Bratic or from Biorcevic because at meetings and briefings, my commanding officer, whom I was driving, always went.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And isn't it the case that, in fact, the situation was that under normal circumstances, Radovan Stojicic, Badza's position was that orders had to pass through him, orders from the JNA had to pass through him, to your unit commander. Isn't that the situation?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Well, some orders were directly received from the Yugoslav People's Army while we were in the area of Vera and Brsadin. Other assignments that had to do with police work, we received from Mr. Radovan Stojicic, Badza. He issued those orders to my commander and the commanding cadre of my unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, to the extent that orders did pass through Radovan Stojicic, Badza, that doesn't reflect that he has a higher authority than the JNA. It just reflects the chain of command, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Well, according to the rules of service in the Yugoslav People's Army, the chain of command should have been completely different. While serving in the Yugoslav People's Army and serving as a driver to my commander, when I was doing my military service in Capljina, I learned it differently during training. However, in the field mission in Western Srem and Baranja, the situation was rather messy. Because, in addition to the Yugoslav People's Army, there was the Serbian Volunteer Guard of Mr. Zeljko Raznjatovic. There was also the Territorial Defence of western --

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, I'm sorry to interrupt you. I will come to Arkan, but at the moment, I just want to focus on the chain of command of your unit. So let's just focus on that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we please bring up 04643, which is Prosecution tab 12. Could we have page 6807, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, sir, the passage is coming up on the screen in front of you but I'll begin reading while that happens. You were asked: "Q. So JNA, the JNA commander, such as Major-General Bratic, commander of the Novi Sad Corps, would give orders to your unit concerning combat, and those orders had to be approached by Stojicic; correct? "A. They would be passed on to the commands of our units." Is that how it was, that such orders were given to Badza and Badza would pass those orders down to you? Your unit.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Well, from what I learnt while driving my commander to a meeting with Badza, our commanding cadre received orders from Badza, whereas in the field, we would make certain adjustments in co-operation with the Yugoslav People's Army, where we were involved together in combat operations, depending on the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So are you saying that sometimes you received direct orders from the JNA commanders in the field, and sometimes you received orders through Badza from the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And the fact that the JNA officers may take care and expend effort to consult with Radovan Stojicic at meetings, that in no way undermines the command relationship between the JNA and Radovan Stojicic, does it?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And you did your basic training and your compulsory military service with the JNA. Do you know that if someone commits a crime while serving in the JNA or the TO that they are subject to military jurisdiction?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Well, if a person commits a crime, that person falls within the military jurisdiction. In my view, the problem in the area was the fact that it was still the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia where the state itself or, rather, the Presidency of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia never proclaimed a state of war or -- or a state of emergency, in any of the territories.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, as a matter of fact, sir, they did. On the 1st of October of 1991. But regardless of whether you have a declaration of war, when you have individuals who are serving in the TO or the JNA and commit crimes while so serving, isn't it understood by everyone that those individuals would be subject to military criminal jurisdiction?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: They fall within the authority of military jurisdiction. But, in that territory, there were no military courts that may have undertaken certain steps in those matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now let's move to Arkan. Did Arkan or other members of the Serbian Volunteer Guard attend daily meetings with senior JNA officers, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Well, as far as I know, there were cases when they attended meetings of the command cadre of the JNA. Activities were discussed in certain territories at those meetings, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Not just some cases. Such meetings were held every evening, were they not?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't know that they took place every evening. I wasn't there every evening. I didn't go to the centre where the Serbian Volunteers Guard members were billeted. We did go, however, when the commander told us to do so. As to what the command of the Serbian Novi Sad Corps and the Territorial Defence did, I don't know. I don't know if they held daily meetings or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we go back on the document on the screen to page 6801, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, down at the bottom of the page, your answer during the Stanisic case was: "A meeting was held every evening, attended by JNA officers, as well, deployed in the area, and agreements were reached between Mr. Radovan Stojicic, Badza, commanders of the Serbian Volunteer Guard, the territorial units deployed there, and our units." Does that refresh your memory that there were meetings every evening at which these issues were discussed?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Well, daily reports were handed over every day. But it was not my commander Sljukic that I drove there. Stevo Pakovic [phoen] also went there. Captain Sljukic went there. Whatever obligations they had, certain officers went to those meetings, or they reported in writing to the command as to what had been done during the day, what had been accomplished during the day, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure I understand your answer. Do you confirm your prior testimony or do you now say it's not true or accurate?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: What I'm saying is that meetings were held every evening. And whether my officers attended them or whether they delivered written reports and dispatches to the superior command, I don't know. In any case, reports had to be delivered every day or, alternatively, officers from my unit would go to attend those meetings. Very often my commander, Zarko Sljukic attended those meetings as well, but that depended on his whereabouts at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And in practice, Arkan and the JNA acted together in operations on a daily basis; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Well, they did not act together on a daily basis. I mean, the Serbian Volunteers Guard and the JNA. There were cases when the JNA only opened artillery fire, and that excluded infantry attacks or similar things. In concert with the JNA and other units, plans were drafted for joint activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we have 026 -- let me restate that number. 02767, Prosecution tab 6, page 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: While we're waiting for that, Mr. Gosnell. The transcript of the other case you were showing, the previous one, which case was that?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: That's the Stanisic and Simatovic case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Stanisic and Simatovic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, sir, coming up on the screen in front you is a statement which you gave on 24th and 25th of August, 2009. I say it's a statement because at the end you signed it. And paragraph 12, which is about to come up on the screen, says: "Since the war started, the JNA and the SDG co-operated on a daily basis. JNA artillery would shell villages and towns and then the SDG would enter the village like infantry." Does that remind you that that's the way it was?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I said that there were no daily combat activities in the area. There was artillery fire which was returned by the Croatian Guards and the MUP, particularly from Nustar. Fire was opened from there on the Brsadin silo where we were, and on village Vera.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Okay. So try to focus on my question. Are you saying that what's in your statement is incorrect?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: What I'm saying is that this is correct. When there was combat, when there was attack on settled areas, the infantry of the JNA participated in co-operation with the Territorial Defence and the SDG.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we have 04640. Prosecution tab 9, please. 04640.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kovacevic, do you remember previously giving testimony about having seen Jovica Stanisic at the Erdut training centre? I don't ask you to recapitulate your evidence, just do you remember having given evidence about it.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we go, please, to page 2166.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, sir, what I'll suggest to you is that you've given radically different accounts about this, and I'm less interested in the differences in your accounts as I am in trying to understand why and how your accounts changed. And this is going to lead me, just so you know, to a discussion about your notes which we discovered from the Prosecution last night at 7.30 apparently have been destroyed. But as a preamble to that, I want you to look closely at the passages I am about to put to you to see how your testimony has changed. Now, at page 19 and I'll read it -- excuse me, at line 19, and I'm going to read this so listen carefully. This was during your initial appearance when you gave your direct examination testimony in the Stanisic case and that was in August 2009. So it was after your Perisic testimony. And you said -- or the question that were asked was: "Can you tell the Court when you did see him for the first time? "A. I cannot remember the exact date, but I think I saw him for the first time in 1991. "Q. And where did you see Mr. Stanisic at that time? "A. I saw him for the first time in the centre of Erdut. "Q. Can you please describe the occasion or the event at which you did see Mr. Stanisic in Erdut in 1991? "A. I drove my superior to a meeting in Erdut to see Mr. Badza. I was standing next to my car together with Captain Zeljko Sucic when a vehicle came by." Before we go further, can I just ask you, that should be Sljukic; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: No. Mr. Zarko Sljukic had already gone to Mr. Radovan Stojicic, Badza, and Captain Zeljko Sucic remained standing by my car together with two soldiers who were on his escort detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So this is a separate person from Sljukic. It's a person named Sucic. Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. At that moment he was by the car, together with me and the other two soldiers I've mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And continuing on, you say: "Some people came out and Captain Sucic told me that Jovica Stanisic has arrived. "Q. Did you hear from Captain Sucic or from anyone else about the purpose of Stanisic arriving in Erdut? "A. He did not say anything about that. I supposed it was because of a meeting or an agreement that was to be discussed. "Q. Was Mr. Stanisic arriving on his own or with other people? "A. I think there were other -- three or four people accompanying him."

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now if we could please have 04643, which is Prosecution tab 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, you'll remember, Mr. Kovacevic, that there was an interval of one year between your direct examination and your cross-examination in the Stanisic case. And when you returned after that one year, at page 6765, here was the testimony that you gave on cross-examination. Down at line 23: "Q. Right. You never saw him," and this is referring to Jovica Stanisic, "in Erdut at any time, did you? "A. I never saw Mr. Jovica Stanisic at Erdut. "Q. Well, when you gave evidence a year ago in this court, on oath, you claimed that you'd seen him in Erdut in 1991. And yet you have a very clear recollection today of not seeing him in Erdut. What's the truth? "A. In 1991, as I was driving my superiors to the meeting in Erdut, I was told that Jovica Stanisic was there as well. However, when I got back home from my testimony, I went through my notes and realised that this was not true. And once my notes are delivered to the Prosecution, this will become quite apparent." Now can I just ask you, sir, is that correct, that after your testimony in August 2009, you returned home, you reviewed some notes, and you realised that the testimony that you had given was incorrect?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: You're saying here August 1991. It was actually in 2009. In August 1991, I didn't return home. I returned home after having appeared in The Hague in 2009. That's when I got home.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: It's possible there was a mistranslation, Mr. Kovacevic. Indeed, after you returned home in August 2009, did you review your notes and did reviewing those notes indicate or suggest to you that you had made an error in your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: When I reviewed my notes in 2009, I realised that I had not seen Mr. Jovica Stanisic personally in 1991 in Erdut. I realised that I had heard from Captain Sucic that Jovica Stanisic was also attending that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, sir, you never testified that you yourself saw -- or you never testified that you yourself identified the individual whom you saw as Mr. Stanisic. What you testified to in your direct examination in August 2009 was that you saw some individuals arrive and that this Captain Sucic told you that one of them was Jovica Stanisic; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. A vehicle arrived. It was Puch vehicle. It was blue. Three or four persons got out. Captain Zeljko Sucic told me that one of them was Mr. Jovica Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, let's go to page 6770. And sometimes Judges are better at putting questions than counsel, and Judge Orie puts the matter, I would suggest to you, rather succinctly. And here's how he puts it, starting at 6770: "Mr. Kovacevic, Mr. Jordash seeks the following to be clarified. Last year in this courtroom you said," and then he repeats what you said, "'and Captain Sucic told me that Jovica Stanisic had arrived.' That's your testimony of last year. "Now, today, you tell that the visit of Mr. Stanisic to the Erdut camp, that you heard about that in a conversation that you had with Miletic in the village of Vera. These are two different stories. What Mr. Jordash want to know is whether you -- which one, if any, is the truth." And then your answer: "Captain Zeljko Sucic told me at the time that Mr. Jovica Stanisic had arrived and then he went on to attend the meeting. Then, as he came out of the meeting and returned to our camp, Mr. Zeljko told me that he was mistaken, that Mr. Jovica Stanisic had not been present there at the time. Now I learned later on from Mr. Veljko Miletic, who regularly attended meetings at Erdut and Dalj, that Jovica Stanisic had been present, though I myself did not see him." If we turn the page, 6772, Judge Orie suggests to you that that is the opposite of what you had said during your testimony in 2009. And then you respond: "At that point this was the statement I made. Then, as I returned to Belgrade and looked into my notes - and I had made notes on a daily basis - I realised that this piece of information was untrue." Now I find your explanation a bit puzzling, but does it come to this, that you mistakenly testified in 2009 that Sucic told you that it was Stanisic who was arriving, and then you go through your notes and you see that something else happened, namely that Sucic initially tells you that Stanisic has arrived. Then he contradicts himself and tells you, no, it wasn't Stanisic, but then someone else named Veljko Miletic tells you that indeed it was Stanisic on that occasion. Is that -- does that sum it up correctly?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I said that when we were in Erdut, Captain Sucic told me that Mr. Jovica Stanisic had arrived. I personally didn't see him there. Later on, I was told that he had not attended the meeting. However, when we returned to Vera, in a subsequent conversation with Mr. Veljko Miletic, I learned from him that Mr. Jovica Stanisic had actually attended that meeting. I did not see him personally. But based on what Mr. Zeljko Sucic told me that he was, and then that he wasn't, and then Mr. Miletic who had also attended the meeting, told me that Mr. Jovica Stanisic had actually attended the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So the difference that you realised or the error that you realised you had made was you forgot to mention to the Chamber that Sucic had later corrected himself and you forgot to mention that Miletic was the source of the information about Jovica Stanisic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. First, Mr. Zeljko Sucic said Jovica Stanisic has arrived. I personally didn't see him. In a subsequent conversation he told me that Jovica had not attended the meeting. Later, I spoke to Mr. Zeljko Miletic who confirmed that Mr. Jovica Stanisic had indeed attended that meeting. In other words, I was not in the building. I could not see for myself whether Jovica was there or not. I only learned from Veljko Miletic that Mr. Jovica Stanisic had attended the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Here is the key question: Think back. What was it in your notes that reminded you that that was the way it really was and that your initial testimony had been erroneous? What was in those notes that jogged your memory so specifically?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't remember exactly what my notes contained. It was four years later. In any case, I made notes every day of what had happened that day of the conversations that I'd had with certain persons and officers with whom I closely co-operated in the area where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: When did you start making these notes and when did you finish making these notes?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I can't tell you when exactly I started making those notes, because I can't remember. And I finished making them in 1995 or perhaps 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And you're saying that you made notes on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Well, perhaps not every day, but while I was in Western Slavonia and Baranja, I did make notes every day or every second day. And later on, depending on what I was involved in, on what happened. I did not make regular notes if I was in Serbia, if I was involved in some duties that concerned the Army of Yugoslavia or the MUP of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And you made a note of any significant personages who you met in the course of your time in Croatia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Well, there were all sorts of notes about my officers or, rather, my superior, about Mr. Veljko Miletic, who was the deputy commander of the 91st police station in Pakrac. There were also notes about Mr. Savo Milovanovic, who was the commander of the Territorial Defence in Brsadin, about Mr. Rajko Brtolinac [phoen], who was also the commander of the Territorial Defence on Bijelo Brdo, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we have 064 -- correction, 04642. Prosecution tab 11. And if we could please turn to page 6743. Well, perhaps we could start on 6742, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, while this is coming up, Mr. Kovacevic, I'll start reading so it can be translated. And you're being asked questions about your notes. And apparently you were told by the investigator of the Prosecution to keep your notes before the Perisic case. Is that correct, that a Prosecution investigator told you to keep your notes?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And at the bottom of 6742, you indicate that you brought your notes with you when you gave your statement to the Office of the Prosecutor in August of 2009. And you say: "The Prosecutor didn't ask to see them and I took them back." And then if we turn the page, you say that you didn't bring them with you to the interview with the Prosecution. Is that correct, you didn't take the notes with you to the interview with the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: In 2009, I did not take my notes for the interview with the Prosecution; whereas, in 2003, when I was giving my first statement, I had the notes with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: But you had brought the notes from Belgrade to your hotel room in The Hague; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, let's go down the page: "Q. When you brought the notes in August of last year, did you offer them to the Prosecutor or did you keep them secret? "A. The documents were in my hotel room, and the proofing dealt with a completely different subject which made me completely forget about having these notes with me." So did you bring the notes with you to The Hague or not?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I had not brought the notes with me at that time. I only had some bullet points on paper. If I had brought the notes at that time, I would have handed them to the Chamber, because the Presiding Judge Orie had asked for hem.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, that was later. Judge Orie hadn't asked for them yet as of that date. So you're saying that this was a lie. It wasn't true. You hadn't brought the notes with you to the The Hague for the session, the interview, in August 2009?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: My notes were not with me in 2009. I only had with me the statement I had given in Belgrade and bullet points concerning some events that were in issue in that case. But the notes, that is to say, the diary, was not with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: All right. Let's see how you describe your notes in your testimony, and again this is your testimony during the Stanisic case, under oath, on the 1st of September, 2010. And what you say there is: "I do have the notes and they are at my home to this day. However, I didn't record anything of importance. If I saw Mr. Stanisic or Frenki Simatovic or anyone else on a particular day, I didn't think it was necessary for me to record that. I actually recorded things relating to my time on the front or about delivering certain goods, and I copied these dispatch notes in order to have them with me." Now, Mr. Kovacevic, given that description of your notes, how on earth did that jog your memory that you had given false testimony in August 2009 in the Stanisic case?

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Sorry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gillett.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: -- to intervene. Just in fairness to the witness, because there are different descriptions of the objects in question, and in relation to what my learned colleague was asking about before, the note -- the notes being brought in August 2009, his description is "the documents were in my hotel room," and then where he refers to the notes being at his house, there is an intervening question. And the witness doesn't read English, so I feel it would be fairer to put that all to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, it's as clear as day when you read the transcript that the notes and the documents are the same. There's no difference. Nothing else is being discussed here. It's the notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Well, the witness, today, has made a distinction between notes and bullet points and other documents. That's why I think it is fairer to give a specific recitation of what he said previously and what the questions were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And what -- what would -- what would be fair to the witness, Mr. Gillett, in your position?

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Simply to note that when my learned colleague refers to his description, that he notes there was also this description of documents being in the hotel room, which is in relation to the initial question posed in Stanisic and Simatovic, and then a subsequent question asks him about whether he has the notes and that's where he says: "I do have notes and they're at my home to this day."

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, it really is clear in the context that there is only one set of notes/documents being referred to here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: By all means, there is little use right now to put that particular question to the witness because the answer is -- has been given or the possible answer has been given. And it will be something the Court has to take into account with -- with the transcript and with everything that has been said. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, do you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not understand you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, I -- I just read out a description of -- that you gave in your testimony in the Stanisic case of your notes. Shall I repeat your description of the notes?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: No need.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: All right. And the question is this: Given your description of the content of your notes, namely that they concerned things relating to your time on the front or about delivering certain goods, you didn't think it was necessary to report or record even seeing, as far as you knew at the time, such personages as Mr. Stanisic or Mr. Simatovic, how is it possible that those notes would have jogged your memory about this convoluted explanation about the information you received from Mr. Sucic and Mr. Miletic?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: It's not convoluted. The information I got from Mr. Sucic because I was with him. And as far as Mr. Miletic is concerned, I served together with him, we spent time in the same place for more than 40 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: That -- that wasn't my question, and perhaps my question was too compound and complex, and I apologise for that, Mr. Kovacevic. It's simply this: What in those notes could have jogged your memory about who informed you of what and caused you to realise that you needed to recant the testimony that you had given in 2009?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I cannot tell you precisely now. I don't know how you want me to explain this.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: You had those notes in September 2010, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Did you see them after you returned from your testimony in The Hague, in 2010?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Do you remember that before you were dismissed as a witness by the Trial Chamber in the Stanisic and Simatovic case, they instructed you to supply those notes to the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And we learned last night that the notes have been destroyed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know if the notes were destroyed or they disappeared. I just can't lay my hands on them anymore. I can't find them. Because upon returning from The Hague, I continued to work in my regular job in a public transport company, and I travel a lot, so it happens often that I'm not home for stretches of two months.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, I just asked you, and it's at page 82, line 10 and 11, whether you saw them after you had returned from The Hague and after you had received this instruction from Judge Orie to supply the notes. Is there some reason why you didn't immediately, once you did return to your home and you saw the notes, why didn't you immediately supply them to the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: There is a reason. I was at home for only two days before leaving on -- on a trip.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Judge Orie instructed you to put the notes in an envelope, seal the envelope, and address it. Even if you didn't have time to deliver it, you couldn't have picked up the telephone and called an official from the ICTY to come and pick them up from you?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. However, upon returning from The Hague, I spent only two days at home before leaving on a trip. I can't remember whether I travelled to Russia or to Siberia. So I was not able to pack it right away. I thought I would do it when I come back from that trip, but then I forgot.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber has indicated that, in the Judgement at page 26 -- excuse me, at paragraph 26 that there were many efforts by the Trial Chamber to receive these notes. Were you aware of these efforts?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Well, possibly I knew -- I probably knew because Judge Orie had ordered it. However, after I left on that trip, my wife told me that they called me once from the field office in Belgrade reminding me to deliver those notes, but I couldn't find those notes later. Maybe my wife put them away somewhere, or my children. In any case, I couldn't find them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Didn't you understand that it was a matter of the utmost importance once you had located those notes again to provide them to the Tribunal, in accordance with an order of the Judges of this Tribunal, to you personally?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But, as I explained, after returning from The Hague, I spent two days at home. On the third day, I left on a trip, and during the first two days I had no time to do it. I just had some rest and left. And after that, it slipped my mind. And later, once my wife told me somebody from the field office called me, but at that point in time, I was no longer able to locate those notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And do you have any other explanation for us about where they might have ended up, how they may have been destroyed? Anything else at all? Or is that it?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether it was during cleaning or tidying up my wife threw them away, or perhaps my son did. Because it was an old notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So somehow that notebook had survived between 1995 and 2010, September 2010, in your possession safely. You saw them. And then suddenly your wife tosses them in the dust bin and they're taken away?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Asked and answered, Mr. Gosnell, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I'll move on, Mr. President. Thank you. Could we have --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us just clear up one thing. I'm not saying my wife put it in the dust bin because in October 2010 we were moving house, and perhaps during the move or after the move, my -- my wife just threw that away.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Did you assist in this moving of house?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: No. Because I wasn't there. I was again on the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: You let your wife move all your belongings, without you being there to assist?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, because I was on the road. My son who was, at that time, 20, was helping her, along with the workers who were paid to move us.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we have the statement back on the screen, please, which is P2027.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you about the meeting that you claim you attended or that you have testified about that occurred at what you describe as Mr. Hadzic's house in Pacetin. Do you remember when that happened? And since there's only one meeting in Pacetin, I think we both know what we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I cannot remember exactly when it was. All I know is that it was before the fall of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And was it after or before the offensive on Brsadin silo?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I seem to remember that it was before the offensive on the Brsadin silo.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And as I understand it, your testimony now is that instead of there being a single meeting at Mr. Hadzic's house, there is an initial meeting at Mr. Hadzic's house and then a second meeting somewhere else; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: When we arrived at Pacetin, I drove my commander to Mr. Hadzic's house. And then later, they moved, I think, to the local commune building at Pacetin.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Did you say that that commune building was nearby the house?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly whether it was nearby the house. But from what I remember, I believe it was in the centre of Pacetin village.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And who was at Mr. Hadzic's house on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: According to what I learned from my commander who was there, Radovan Stojicic, Badza, and other persons were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: What other persons?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly who else was there. There was my commander. The late Radovan Stojicic, Badza. I cannot remember if Mr. Bratic or someone else or Rade Leskovac were there. I can't remember now.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: You say you were told that Radovan Stojicic, Badza, was present. Does that mean you didn't see him yourself with your own eyes?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And by your commander, are you referring to Mr. Sljukic?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we have 1D441, please. Defence tab 27.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: While that's coming up, could you describe the house that you identify as being Mr. Hadzic's house? What was it like?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: The house is right by the street. It had a metal gate, as far as I remember. A large gate, metallic. And another gate in a brick wall and two small windows looking out into the street.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, you say that there's a gate, and then another gate. Does that mean a gate for a driveway so that cars can enter?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So two metal gates leading to two driveways; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: One gate was about 2 and a half or 3 metres wide, and there was a narrow gate for pedestrians only.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And how many buildings were part of this house of Mr. Hadzic that you describe? One building? Two buildings? More?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I did not enter the courtyard. I could only see from the street that it was a house going more into depth than it was wide. And how many rooms it had, I couldn't tell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I suppose while you were waiting outside -- well, let me ask you: Was there anyone else waiting outside -- were you waiting outside the house?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I was parked, perhaps, 50 metres from the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Why so far away?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: There were already one or two cars parked there when I arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: One or two cars are parked there, and then you have to park 50 metres away? I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Since the cars were already parked by the pavement, I parked 20 metres away, perhaps, from them. So I was about 50 metres away from the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: On the screen in front of you is an overview, an aerial view of Pacetin. Are you able to identify where Mr. Hadzic's house was located?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: On this map, I could not tell because I came by the dirt track from the direction of Vera.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: This is a village with -- it appears you could miss in the blink of an eye. There are two cross-roads. What difference does it make whether you came on a dirt track or came from any direction at all?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that village has two major intersections and about three or four streets, all in all. I cannot pin-point exactly where it was, but I believe that I took a right turn at the first intersection from the dirt track that took me to about halfway through the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And Vera is to the north of Pacetin; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: That's the direction you came from, correct, to the north, or from the north?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But I did not take the asphalt road but the dirt track.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Why didn't you take the asphalt road?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: We did not because it was targeted from the village of Nustar.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: You're saying the dirt road wasn't equally targeted?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: No. The dirt road was not targeted. Only the asphalt road.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Isn't the front line to the south of this image, along the river Vuka? At least for some stretch of the front line.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: The infantry weapons was not an issue. It was targeted from artillery weapons. And tanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Are you in any way capable of identifying the road, the dirt road, that leads into Pacetin that you say that you took that day? Take a close look at this image and see if it helps you.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Whether we arrived between the plots of land on this dirt road, I can't remember exactly. But we did arrive from Vera along a dirt road.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So you can't identify either Mr. Hadzic's house or the second location where you say there was a second meeting; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: The second location was in the centre of the village. As for Mr. Hadzic's house, I don't know its exact location. If you were to show me a photo of the house, I'm sure that I would recognise it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I see that's the time for today, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: It is, Mr. Gosnell. Thank you. Mr. Kovacevic, this is the end of the today -- of the hearing today. We -- you will come back tomorrow at night -- at 9.00. You're not released as a witness, and that means that, in the meantime, you probably know the drill, in the meantime, you can't discuss your testimony with anyone, and you're not allowed to talk to ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Madam Registrar. We'll talk about -- we'll talk about the exact timing in a moment. But between now and the moment you come back, you cannot talk to anybody about -- discuss your testimony with anybody, nor can you talk to any of the parties. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, as for the moment you would come back, it is not tomorrow at 9.00. Tomorrow we have two videolink witnesses that we have to start with. So either you will come back tomorrow at the end of the hearing, somewhere in the end of the hearing, or even on Wednesday, on Wednesday morning. We will see about that. Thank you. The court usher will escort you out of the courtroom now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Sorry to detain us any longer, Mr. President. But we gave a foreshadowing of this request in an e-mail on, I think, Sunday, and now I can say confidentially that I certainly could use an additional hour for this witness. So our application would be one additional hour for cross-examination, thus increasing from three to four. I'm not quite sure where we stand now, in terms of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: 2:18. Two hours, 18 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Anything from the Defence on that request -- from the -- sorry, from the OTP on that request?

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: No. We take no position on that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The request is granted. Nothing else? Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 11th day of June, 2013, at 9.00 a.m.
